exit_trigger: Evidence of moat erosion, such as loss of pricing power or loss of key OEM or customer qualifications; Electrification or other technology shifts materially shrinking the addressable additive market faster than the business can adapt; Management failure, dishonesty, or value-destroying acquisitions or buybacks; Price rising above 1.5x a conservatively haircut intrinsic value, with the gap persisting; Debt-to-equity moving clearly above the current 0.497
rationale: I own this one, and the price is 21% below what we paid. A lower price on a business whose competitive position hasn't changed is not a reason to sell; it is a reason to read the file more carefully. The snapshot shows a five-year average ROE of 30.6%, debt-to-equity of 0.497 and a market cap of about $6.6 billion, and the model's own value of about $1,272 a share leaves a margin of safety near 45%. I don't take that at face value, because it rests on 8% growth capped from a 13.9% trailing rate and a 5% discount rate, and I would haircut both. The snapshot does not give me earnings history, management tenure or insider activity, so I can't call this a full conviction add. I keep the share, I don't chase it, and I sell only if the moat erodes, not because Mr. Market is sulking.

exit_trigger: Evidence of erosion in brand pricing power, such as sustained discounting to move product; Persistent loss of market share to rivals in its core category; Management destroying value through poor acquisitions or buybacks at inflated prices; Evidence of dishonesty or accounting problems; Price above 1.5x a conservatively verified intrinsic value
rationale: I own ten shares, bought at $128.38 in August and now marked at $111.23, down 13.36%. A price decline alone is no reason to sell if the business is intact, and nothing in this snapshot says the moat has cracked. The numbers I can see are excellent: 5-year average ROE of 34.6%, debt-to-equity of 0.0, and 5-year average owner earnings of about $1.32 billion against a $12.3 billion market cap. The model's $347 value rests on 8% growth and a 5% discount rate, so I treat it as a ceiling, not a target. My worry is that apparel is fashion-driven, and a brand that must be rebuilt every season is no moat at all. So I keep the position and do not add until I can verify the earnings record and the management record. Being wrong about the brand would cost me more than the price decline already has.

exit_trigger: Franchise protection laws are weakened and manufacturers can sell direct to consumers at scale; Service and parts gross profit declines persistently, showing the recurring-income base is eroding; Management makes value-destroying acquisitions or buys back stock far above intrinsic value; Debt-to-equity rises materially above 0.5; Price rises above 1.5x intrinsic value and stays there
rationale: I own this one, and the question is whether to keep it, not whether to open it. It is a car and truck dealer, a business I understand. Selling cars and servicing them is not glamorous, but I have owned dealerships before and know how they earn their money. The numbers I can see are sound. Five-year average ROE is 23.8%, debt-to-equity is 0.39, and owner earnings of about $1.09 billion put my value near $259.62 against a price of $213.01, a margin of safety of about 18%. But the moat is thinner than I would like, resting mostly on franchise protections and scale, and I cannot check ten years of earnings, management tenure or insider activity from this snapshot. So I keep the shares, I do not add on a case this unproven, and I stay ready to sell if the franchise protection erodes. We are down about 1.7% after 94 days, which is noise to me.

exit_trigger: Evidence of moat erosion, such as sustained loss of share to e-commerce or lower-cost distributors; Return on equity falling durably below 15%; Management capital allocation failure, such as overpriced acquisitions; Price above 1.5x intrinsic value with a persistent gap
rationale: I own 11 shares of MSM, bought two weeks ago at $120.05, and they are down about 1.9% — a rounding error against a business I intend to own for years. The snapshot shows a 5-year average ROE of 20.0% and a debt-to-equity of 0.35, both comfortably inside my thresholds. On 5-year average owner earnings of about $303 million, with growth capped at 8% and a 5% discount rate, I get roughly $157 a share against a $117.75 price — a 25% margin of safety, above my 15% bar. I could not verify from this snapshot the ten-year earnings record, CEO tenure, or the cost-advantage evidence behind the moat, so I am not adding on this evidence alone. A price decline with the thesis intact is no reason to sell, so I keep what I own and stay patient.

exit_trigger: Evidence that brand pricing power is eroding, with falling margins and share loss to heat pump or tankless rivals; Management makes value-destroying acquisitions or buys back stock at prices far above intrinsic value; Price exceeds 1.5× intrinsic value and the gap persists; A significantly better opportunity at much higher conviction
rationale: I own this one, 21 shares bought 17 days ago at $61.505, and it is up about 5.2% since. A water heater and boiler maker is a business I can describe in two paragraphs, and the snapshot shows a 5-year average ROE of 23.7% with debt-to-equity of only 0.083. At $64.72 against a conservative owner-earnings value of $95.72, the margin of safety is 32.4%, well beyond the 15% I require. But the snapshot does not give me ten years of earnings history, CEO tenure or insider activity, so I cannot tick every box, and my confidence stays moderate. A 17-day-old position is no reason to sell and no reason to chase. I keep it, let the owner earnings compound, and add only if the price falls with the moat intact.

exit_trigger: Evidence of brand pricing power eroding, such as sustained inability to pass through costs without losing volume; Management making value-destroying acquisitions or acting dishonestly; Debt rising materially above the very low level reported in the snapshot; Price persistently above 1.5 times intrinsic value; A much higher-conviction opportunity that requires funding
rationale: I own these shares, and eleven days in I see no reason to change my mind. This is a maker of coatings, sealants and repair products that people buy in small tickets and rarely think twice about. The snapshot shows a five-year average ROE of 22.9% and a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.0027, and I would want to check that debt figure against the filing because it looks strikingly low. The model puts value at $133.59 against a price of $104.76, a 21.6% margin of safety, which clears my 15% bar. But the 5% discount rate and 8% growth cap flatter that number, and I could not verify ten years of earnings, CEO tenure or insider activity from this snapshot, so I will hold what I have and not chase it. Time is the friend of the wonderful company, and I will let it work.

exit_trigger: Evidence that its cost or scale advantage has eroded against competitors or imports; Earnings turning negative or falling significantly over a multi-year stretch; Management destroying value through poor acquisitions or buybacks at inflated prices; Debt turning out to be materially higher than the reported 0.0 debt-to-equity suggests; Price exceeding 1.5x a conservatively re-derived intrinsic value, with the gap persisting
rationale: I own 24 shares, bought four days ago at $54.285, and the position is up about 1% - far too early to say anything about the decision except that the numbers I can see are good. Return on equity averaged 29.3% over five years, the snapshot shows debt-to-equity of 0.0, and market cap is about $6.1 billion, so size is fine. The model's $168.53 of value per share rests on 8% growth and a 5% discount rate, which is generous for what I understand to be a metal-fabricating business, so I discount that 67% margin of safety heavily. The snapshot gives me no ten-year earnings record, no ROIC, no CEO tenure and no insider data, so I can't confirm those criteria, and my moat conviction is modest because this is an input-cost-driven industry. I keep the shares and don't add until I can verify a durable cost advantage and steady earnings through the cycle.

exit_trigger: Not applicable, no position held; Would revisit if a durable moat can be evidenced and a 10-year earnings record verified
rationale: I don't own Skyworks, and on this evidence I'm not going to start. The numbers in front of me look good: a 5-year average ROE of 19.1%, debt-to-equity of 0.086, and a snapshot margin of safety of 27.6% against an intrinsic value of $115.40. But a cheap-looking price is not a moat. Radio-frequency chips for handsets are a fast-changing business with a concentrated customer base, and I can't tell you with confidence what they'll look like in ten years. I can't describe that durable advantage in two honest paragraphs, so I'll sit on my hands and keep watching. Charlie would say to invert: what would have to go wrong? Here, the answer is a rival design win at a single large customer, and I can't rule that out.
